title: #HackAVP CV FORGE L'USINE A CV BOOSTÉE PAR IA LOCALE
summary:
J’ai transformé ma RTX 4060 en usine à CV grâce à une IA locale

Comment j’ai construit, chez moi, une brique d’extraction de CV on-premise avec OCR, Ollama, Qwen, Pydantic, JSON Resume et Europass.

TL;DR

Dans le cadre de HackAVP 2026, j’ai développé CV Forge, une brique capable de transformer un CV en données structurées réutilisables par d’autres services.

Ce projet s’inscrit dans un écosystème local porté par plusieurs acteurs :

  • OPT-NC, à l’origine du besoin et des données du challenge,
  • Station N, pour le cadre d’innovation et le challenge HackAVP,
  • l’IAE / Université de la Nouvelle-Calédonie, pour l’accompagnement pédagogique,
  • et mon entreprise BARRAU BUSINESS SYSTEME, qui m’a permis de développer mes compétences jusqu’à pouvoir construire cette solution.

L’objectif de CV Forge est simple : extraire, interpréter, valider et standardiser les informations contenues dans un CV afin de les rendre exploitables par d’autres briques HackAVP.

Vidéo :

Écosystème du projet

Le défi : un CV n’est pas une base de données

Un humain lit un CV presque instantanément.

Il repère naturellement :

  • le nom du candidat,
  • ses expériences,
  • ses diplômes,
  • ses compétences,
  • ses coordonnées.

Mais pour une machine, le problème est beaucoup plus compliqué.

Un CV peut être :

  • en une ou deux colonnes,
  • très graphique,
  • composé d’images,
  • exporté depuis Word, Canva ou un autre outil,
  • organisé différemment d’un document à l’autre.

Le problème est donc double : extraire le contenu du document, puis comprendre ce contenu sans inventer d’informations. Une mauvaise extraction ne devient pas correcte simplement parce qu'elle passe dans un LLM.

🏠 Mon laboratoire IA : du on-premise chez moi

J'ai choisi d'héberger ma solution sur mon ordinateur perso. Les CV comportent des informations personnelles : identité, coordonnées, formations et parcours professionnel. Exécuter l'OCR et le modèle d'IA localement me permet de maîtriser le traitement sans envoyer ces documents à une API d'IA cloud.

Cela ne veut pas dire que le on-premise est automatiquement sécurisé ou conforme au RGPD. Il faut aussi protéger les accès, les fichiers et les journaux, et définir des règles de conservation. En revanche, je maîtrise mieux mon environnement et je peux expérimenter sans facturation par requête.

Mon setup

Composant Choix
GPU NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060
VRAM 8 Go
Prix de ma carte en Nouvelle-Calédonie Environ 60 000 F CFP
Hébergement Local, chez moi
Moteur IA Ollama
Modèle Qwen léger 3 4B
Services Python / FastAPI
Validation Pydantic
Orchestration n8n
Format d'échange JSON Resume
Autre format ciblé Europass

Je n'ai pas essayé de faire tourner le modèle le plus volumineux possible. J'ai sélectionné une approche adaptée à mon besoin : identifier et structurer des données de CV.

Le défi n'est pas de disposer du plus gros GPU, mais de tirer le meilleur parti de celui que j'ai.

⚙️ Sous le capot : de l'OCR au JSON Resume

J'ai découpé mon traitement en briques spécialisées. Chacune a sa propre responsabilité : extraire, interpréter, valider, puis partager.

  1. Le workflow n8n reçoit le CV à traiter.
  2. Un service OCR / extraction récupère les informations du document.
  3. Le contenu extrait est analysé par Qwen via Ollama, exécuté localement.
  4. Le résultat est normalisé selon une structure attendue.
  5. Pydantic contrôle les types, la structure et certaines règles métier.
  6. Le profil est transformé en JSON Resume.
  7. Ce format peut être consommé par les autres services HackAVP et servir de point de départ à une conversion Europass.

Diagramme de séquence du traitement

Pourquoi séparer les services ?

Je ne veux pas que le modèle d'IA fasse tout car on ne peux pas le faire confiance à 100 % : l'OCR est chargé d'extraire, Qwen d'interpréter, Pydantic de valider la structure et le convertisseur de produire un format d'échange. Cette modularité permet de remplacer un composant sans réécrire l'ensemble de la chaîne, tant que ses interfaces restent compatibles.

🧪 Banc d'essai : une RTX 4060 face à une RTX 5080

Mes collègues chargé de CV Generator utilisent une RTX 5080 avec 16 Go de VRAM. Sa machine peut accueillir des modèles plus volumineux, selon la quantification et la mémoire nécessaire, ce qui peut être intéressant pour la génération de documents et certaines tâches de compréhension plus complexes.

Exécution On-premise On-premise

Un modèle plus grand peut mieux réussir certaines tâches et produire moins d'erreurs, mais ce n'est pas automatique : il faut le vérifier avec les mêmes documents et les mêmes critères, même si les erreurs sont moins présente. Une carte plus puissante n'élimine pas magiquement les hallucinations.

Et si je change de GPU demain ?

L'architecture peut monter en puissance. Avec davantage de VRAM, je pourrais tester des modèles plus gros tout en conservant le même enchaînement :

OCR → Ollama / Qwen → Pydantic → JSON Resume → Autres applications

Il faudrait bien sûr adapter la configuration, vérifier les performances et retester la précision. Mais on ne repart pas de zéro : le principe de séparation des composants reste le même.

Aujourd'hui je privilégie une IA spécialisée sur du matériel accessible. Demain je peux faire évoluer le matériel et le modèle, sans renoncer au format d'échange.

🔧 Retour d'expérience : stop aux rustines !

Pendant le développement, j'ai parfois tenté de corriger les erreurs en ajoutant des nœuds n8n, des conditions ou des instructions au prompt.

Le problème ? À force de donner des coups de clé à molette, le workflow devient une usine à gaz ! 😅

Avec ma RTX 4060, il faut que j'accepte les limites du LLM, on ne peut pas forcer une imprimante à faire de la vidéo, il faut upgrade ses composants.

🐛 Un exemple concret

Sur certains CV, mon pipeline retrouvait :

  • ✅ Les expériences professionnelles
  • ✅ Les formations et compétences
  • ✅ Les coordonnées
  • ❌ Mais parfois… pas le nom du candidat !

La leçon : identifier si l'erreur vient de l'OCR, du modèle ou de la validation avant d'ajouter un correctif.

💡 Dix rustines ne transformeront jamais un petit LLM en modèle booster. Mieux vaut une architecture propre et évolutive qu'une accumulation de correctifs.

✅ Qualité des données : une IA sous contrôle

Avec mon modèle Qwen, j'obtiens des résultats encourageants et peu d'erreurs visibles sur les CV.

Mais une IA peut toujours halluciner ! C'est pourquoi je contrôle plusieurs points :

  • ✅ Structure : JSON conforme grâce à Pydantic.
  • 🎯 Exactitude : informations fidèles au CV original.
  • 📄 Complétude : données essentielles récupérées.
  • ⚡ Performance : environ 44 secondes sur un test.

Un JSON valide ne signifie pas forcément que les informations sont exactes !

🔗 HackAVP : l'interopérabilité avant tout !

Le véritable enseignement de HackAVP ? Faire communiquer plusieurs applications indépendantes autour d'un objectif commun.

Avec CV Forge, je transforme les CV en JSON Resume, un format standardisé que les autres équipes peuvent directement exploiter.

🔄 Un format, plusieurs possibilités

  • 📄 CV Forge → Extraction et structuration.
  • 🎯 CV Matching → Correspondance candidat/poste.
  • ✍️ CV Generator → Génération de candidatures.
  • 🇪🇺 Europass → Interopérabilité avec un standard européen.

Chaque brique possède sa propre technologie, mais toutes peuvent communiquer grâce à un format de données commun.

Europass : ne pas s'enfermer dans HackAVP

J'ai aussi travaillé sur une correspondance des champs vers le modèle de données Europass : identité, expériences, formations, langues et compétences.

Cette approche permet d'envisager la réutilisation des profils au-delà de notre écosystème. Il s'agit d'un travail de compatibilité des structures de données, pas que d'une certification officielle Europass. La validation exhaustive des exports est un point à poursuivre.

L'interopérabilité, ce n'est pas seulement réussir une requête HTTP. C'est permettre à des systèmes conçus séparément de partager une information qui garde le même sens.

Et c'est aussi une question d'architecture : si demain je change mon GPU, mon modèle Qwen ou mon service OCR, les autres équipes ne devraient pas devoir réécrire leurs applications tant que je respecte le contrat de sortie.

🚀 Et après ?

Pour aller plus loin, je souhaite surtout :

  • construire un jeu de CV de test avec des résultats attendus ;
  • mesurer séparément les erreurs OCR, les erreurs de normalisation et les anomalies métier ;
  • comparer plusieurs versions de Qwen sur des documents identiques ;
  • mesurer la latence moyenne et la consommation de VRAM ;
  • améliorer les contrôles sur les champs critiques ;
  • approfondir les tests de conversion vers Europass.

🏁 Conclusion : une IA locale, mais surtout une architecture ouverte

Avec CV Forge, j'ai voulu démontrer qu'une RTX 4060 de 8 Go, un modèle Qwen léger et une chaîne de traitement bien pensée suffisent déjà pour développer une brique d'extraction de CV utile.

Je retiens toutefois un enseignement plus large : la réussite d'un projet ne se résume ni à la taille du modèle, ni au nombre de nœuds n8n. Il faut savoir identifier les limites du matériel, contrôler ses résultats et concevoir des interfaces capables d'évoluer.

Mais mon principal apprentissage reste l'interopérabilité : transformer un document en donnée structurée est une première étape ; permettre à plusieurs applications de s'appuyer sur cette donnée sans dépendre les unes des autres, c'est ce qui donne toute sa valeur au projet.

Le vrai produit de CV Forge n'est pas un nouveau PDF : c'est un profil candidat structuré, contrôlable et réutilisable.

title: FastAPI: idempotencia en emails de prueba
summary:
Las pruebas de registro que dependen de un email suelen fallar de una forma dificil de explicar. El test crea un usuario, solicita un mensaje de verificación y espera una señal. Si la consulta tarda, el runner reintenta. Entonces aparecen dos usuarios, dos mensajes o un resultado que ya no sabemos a qué ejecución pertenece.

En mis scripts de backend, trato cada email de prueba como una operación idempotente. La idea es simple: repetir la misma petición debe devolver el mismo resultado lógico, aunque el proveedor tarde o la automatización pierda una respuesta. Esto hace que un endpoint para validar emails de prueba sin ruido sea mucho más util en CI.

El problema de repetir una prueba de email

Imagina este flujo:

crear usuario -> pedir verificación -> revisar buzón -> confirmar usuario

Un timeout entre “pedir verificación” y “revisar buzón” no significa que la primera operación no ocurrió. Sin un identificador estable, el test no puede distinguir entre una petición pendiente y una nueva petición. La reaccion habitual es repetir todo el flujo, y ahi nace el duplicado.

Hay dos claves para evitarlo:

  • El cliente envía una clave de idempotencia por ejecución.
  • El servidor guarda el estado y el resultado asociado a esa clave.

La clave no debe ser el email solamente. Un mismo buzón puede servir para varias ejecuciones y una prueba nueva necesita su propio contexto. Una combinación como run_id + caso_de_prueba suele ser suficiente para empezar.

Un contrato idempotente para el endpoint

El endpoint puede aceptar una petición pequeña y explicita:

{
  "email": "qa-42@example.test",
  "test_case": "signup_verification",
  "idempotency_key": "run-2026-10-20-42"
}

Para la misma idempotency_key, la API debería devolver uno de estos resultados:

  • 201 created si acaba de registrar la solicitud.
  • 200 existing si la solicitud ya estaba completa.
  • 202 pending si sigue en proceso y todavía no hay resultado final.
  • 409 conflict si la clave se reutilizó con un email o caso diferente.

El 409 es importante. Si una clave cambia de significado en mitad de una prueba, ocultar el problema detrás de un 200 produce diagnósticos confusos. Un mensaje de error claro ahorra bastante tiempo despues.

Implementación pequeña con FastAPI

Para una prueba local no hace falta construir un sistema enorme. Un repositorio en memoria permite probar el contrato antes de elegir PostgreSQL o Redis:

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr

app = FastAPI()
requests: dict[str, dict] = {}


class VerificationRequest(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr
    test_case: str
    idempotency_key: str


@app.post("/verification-requests")
def create_request(payload: VerificationRequest):
    saved = requests.get(payload.idempotency_key)
    if saved:
        same_input = (
            saved["email"] == str(payload.email)
            and saved["test_case"] == payload.test_case
        )
        if not same_input:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=409, detail="Clave reutilizada")
        return {"status": "existing", **saved}

    record = {
        "email": str(payload.email),
        "test_case": payload.test_case,
        "status": "pending",
    }
    requests[payload.idempotency_key] = record
    return {"status": "created", **record}

Cómo conectar la automatización sin duplicados

La automatización puede separar tres pasos: reservar la solicitud, esperar la señal y confirmar el resultado. Cada paso consulta el estado existente antes de hacer trabajo nuevo.

def wait_for_verification(client, key: str, timeout: float = 30):
    request = client.get(f"/verification-requests/{key}")
    if request["status"] == "confirmed":
        return request

    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        message = client.find_message(key=key)
        if message:
            return client.confirm(key=key, message_id=message["id"])
        time.sleep(1)

    return {"status": "pending", "key": key}

Si el equipo necesita generar un correo desechable, esa acción debe quedar fuera de la clave de idempotencia o asociarse a ella de forma explícita. De lo contrario, un reintento puede reservar otro buzón y perder el mensaje original. En mis notas he visto nombres como temp mailid y temp org mail; aunque parezcan equivalentes, conviene conservar el identificador que realmente devolvió el adaptador.

También es útil registrar created_at, expires_at, message_id y un código de error del proveedor. No guardaría el contenido completo del mensaje si sólo se necesita verificar un token. Menos datos hacen el debugging mas seguro y reducen el ruido en los logs.

Preguntas rápidas

¿Una clave de idempotencia debe durar para siempre?

No. Debe durar lo suficiente para cubrir los reintentos de la ejecución. Un TTL evita que el almacén crezca sin limite y permite reutilizar nombres de pruebas antiguas con un nuevo run_id.

¿Qué hacemos si el mensaje llega después del timeout?

Marca el caso como pending o expired, pero conserva la evidencia. Un proceso de limpieza puede retirar el buzón y el runner puede decidir si reintenta toda la prueba. No conviertas un timeout en “email inexistente” sin comprobar el estado del proveedor.

No. Este patrón mejora la confiabilidad del flujo y hace sus fallos más legibles. Todavía conviene tener algunas pruebas end-to-end con un proveedor real y otras unitarias con un adaptador falso.

  • [ ] La clave de idempotencia combina ejecución y caso de prueba.
  • [ ] Reutilizar la clave con datos distintos devuelve 409.
  • [ ] La base de datos protege la inserción concurrente.
  • [ ] pending, expired y provider_error son estados distintos.
  • [ ] El token o contenido sensible no aparece en logs.
  • [ ] El cleanup conoce la caducidad del buzón y de la solicitud.

En mis scripts de backend, trato cada email de prueba como una operación idempotente. La idea es simple: repetir la misma petición debe devolver el mismo resultado lógico, aunque el proveedor tarde o la automatización pierda una respuesta. Esto hace que un endpoint para validar emails de prueba sin ruido sea mucho más util en CI.

El problema de repetir una prueba de email

Imagina este flujo:

  • El servidor guarda el estado y el resultado asociado a esa clave.

title: Monitoring My Flask App with Prometheus and Grafana
summary:
Introduction

For an earlier IT 3200 assignment, I built a small Flask app and ran it in Docker on a Linux virtual machine. The app displays a simple HTML page. For this assignment, I added monitoring so I could see how many requests it received, whether any requests failed, and how long the app took to respond.

I used Google Compute Engine to host the app, Prometheus to collect metrics, and Grafana to display them. I tested the setup by sending requests to the app and checking whether the graphs changed.

Everything runs on one Linux VM called vm-it3200-m7. It has three Docker containers: student-app, prometheus, and grafana. This was a small class project, so I kept the setup on one server.

Why Prometheus and Grafana?

I chose Prometheus because I had already used it in the Cloud Watching assignment. It checks a metrics endpoint at regular intervals and saves the numbers over time. Its query language, PromQL, lets me look at things like request counts and response times. Those were useful measurements for my Flask app.

I added Grafana so I could see several graphs together instead of running each query separately. Prometheus collects and stores the metrics, and Grafana reads that data to build the dashboard.

Google Cloud's monitoring service would have been another option, but Prometheus let me build on the work I had already done. Loki or the Elastic Stack would make more sense if I wanted to search through logs. For this project, I focused on request counts, errors, and response times.

There are limits to this setup. Checking every 15 seconds can miss short problems between checks, and the app's counters reset when its process restarts. I also did not add tracing or a central log system. Since everything is on one VM, a VM failure would take down both the app and its monitoring tools.

Architecture

The firewall rule allows my public IPv4 address using a /32 range and applies to the VM through the it3200-m7 network tag. I used port 3000 for Flask, 9090 for Prometheus, and 3001 for Grafana. Grafana uses port 3000 inside its container, so Docker maps the VM's port 3001 to the container's port 3000.

The containers communicate through a Docker network called it3200-monitoring. Prometheus connects to http://student-app:3000/metrics, and Grafana connects to http://prometheus:9090. Docker lets them find each other by container name, so they do not need to use the VM's public IP to communicate. Someone with administrator access to Docker can still access these containers.

Prometheus saves its data in a Docker volume named prometheus-data and keeps it for two days. Grafana saves its settings in grafana-data. Replacing a container does not erase these volumes, but deleting the VM's storage would. That is why I saved my screenshots and configuration on my computer.

Installation and configuration

First, I installed Docker on the Ubuntu VM:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y docker.io curl
sudo systemctl enable --now docker

My app already had a Dockerfile using Python 3.11. It installs the packages in requirements.txt, copies the app files, and runs python app.py on port 3000. I reused that Dockerfile.

I added this dependency to requirements.txt:

prometheus-flask-exporter==0.23.2

Then I added the exporter right after creating the Flask app:

from flask import Flask, render_template
from prometheus_flask_exporter import PrometheusMetrics

app = Flask(__name__)
metrics = PrometheusMetrics(app, group_by='endpoint')

This adds a /metrics page that Prometheus can read. The group_by setting groups request times by the Flask endpoint instead of every possible URL. The exporter also leaves its own metrics requests out of the default request measurements. Otherwise, checking the app could look like extra user traffic.

I configured Prometheus to check two targets every 15 seconds:

global:
  scrape_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: prometheus
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9090']
  - job_name: flask-app
    metrics_path: /metrics
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['student-app:3000']

The first target is Prometheus itself, which I used for Cloud Watching. The second is my Flask app. One thing I learned was that seeing Prometheus marked UP does not automatically mean it is collecting data from the app too.

I rebuilt the application and created the Docker network:

sudo docker build -t student-app:monitoring .
sudo docker network create it3200-monitoring

I used observability/deploy.sh to start the containers. The script builds the app and checks the Prometheus configuration with promtool check config. It also stops and renames the previous containers so they are kept as backups. The new containers use the shared Docker network and saved data volumes. Docker logs are limited to three 10 MB files per container to help prevent them from filling the disk.

These are the Prometheus settings for the configuration file, storage, and retention:

-v "$PWD/observability/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro"
-v prometheus-data:/prometheus
--config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
--storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus
--storage.tsdb.retention.time=2d

These lines are part of the Docker command, so they should not be run by themselves. The full script is included at the end of this post. If the containers or network already exist, check their names before running the commands again.

I used this file to tell Grafana where to find Prometheus:

apiVersion: 1
datasources:
  - name: Prometheus
    uid: prometheus
    type: prometheus
    access: proxy
    url: http://prometheus:9090
    isDefault: true
    editable: false
    jsonData:
      timeInterval: 15s

Grafana loads this file from /etc/grafana/provisioning/datasources. Another configuration file loads the dashboard JSON from /var/lib/grafana/dashboards. This saves the dashboard setup in files so I can recreate it without setting up every panel by hand.

I included the full script and monitoring files at the end of this post. Each code block shows where to save the file in the app project.

I used the latest Docker tags for Prometheus and Grafana. The script records the downloaded image IDs and digests in deployed-images.txt. Since latest can change, using those recorded digests would be a better way to repeat the setup with the exact same versions.

What the dashboard measures

The dashboard contains five panels:

Panel Purpose
Flask scrape availability Shows whether Prometheus can collect Flask metrics.
Requests per second Shows the rate of application HTTP requests.
HTTP errors per second Shows 4xx and 5xx response rates.
Mean response duration Shows mean server-side request processing time.
Requests by HTTP status Separates cumulative request counters by status code.

Request rate uses:

sum(rate(flask_http_request_total{job="flask-app"}[1m]))

The request counter keeps increasing as requests come in. rate uses the last minute of samples to estimate requests per second. It can account for a counter resetting, but it needs more than one sample before it can show a rate.

Mean response duration uses the histogram's sum and count:

sum(rate(flask_http_request_duration_seconds_sum{job="flask-app"}[1m]))
/
sum(rate(flask_http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="flask-app"}[1m]))

The duration metric measures how long the server takes to process requests. It does not include the full time a browser waits over the internet. The graph can have gaps when there are no requests. I created dashboards for this project but did not set up automatic alerts.

Showing it working

The Docker output shows all three containers running, and the readiness request returns Prometheus Server is Ready.

The up query returned 1 for both Prometheus and Flask, showing that both could be scraped. Grafana is not listed here because it reads data from Prometheus instead of being a scrape target in my setup.

To test it, I sent 120 requests to the home page with a half-second pause between requests. Then I sent ten requests to /missing-page. That page does not exist, so it returns a 404. This gave me a simple way to check whether errors appeared on the dashboard.

for i in $(seq 1 120); do
  curl -fsS http://localhost:3000/ > /dev/null
  sleep 0.5
done

for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000/missing-page
  sleep 1
done

In the screenshot, Flask scrape availability stays at 1 across the displayed samples. Around 22:17, the request rate peaks at about 1.9 requests per second and then drops to about 0.4 as the test finishes. The status graph shows about 120 successful responses and ten 404 responses. These numbers are estimates from reading the graph.

The error graph starts at zero and then rises to about 0.11 errors per second during the missing-page test. The errors were expected because I requested a page that did not exist. The displayed rate is averaged over a one-minute window, which is why it is lower than the one request per second sent by the test.

The average response time is roughly 230–260 microseconds, or 0.23–0.26 milliseconds. Grafana displays these small values in microseconds even though the original metric uses seconds. The requests came from inside the VM and the app is simple, so this does not tell me how fast the app would be for users over the internet or under a much larger load. Empty sections of the rate and duration graphs can also mean there were not enough recent requests or samples.

The graphs matched the activity I generated: the request count increased, the missing-page requests showed up as 404s, and Prometheus continued collecting metrics. Browser visits can add requests too, so I would not expect the counters to match a test script exactly every time.

The updated app also passed three local checks: successful requests were counted and timed, missing pages were counted as 404s, and metrics scrapes did not inflate the app request count. I still needed the VM checks and screenshots to confirm that the containers and dashboard worked together.

Roadblocks and lessons learned

My first roadblock was getting the VM running again. I had deleted the previous Azure resource group to avoid costs. When I tried creating another VM, Azure blocked it because of a subscription region policy. I switched to Google Compute Engine and reused the same Dockerized app.

Another thing I learned was the difference between monitoring Prometheus and monitoring my app. Cloud Watching only needed Prometheus to monitor itself. Adding the Flask exporter and a second target let me see what the app was doing. I also learned why the target uses student-app:3000: inside the Prometheus container, localhost points back to Prometheus, not Flask.

Security and cost considerations

I restricted the firewall rule to my public IPv4 address and the ports needed for the lab. Grafana requires an admin password, and new account sign-ups are disabled. I entered the password when running the script instead of saving it in the code. Someone with Docker administrator access could still inspect container settings, so this is not a complete solution for storing production secrets.

This setup uses HTTP, so restricting the source IP does not encrypt the connection. For a longer-term deployment, I would use HTTPS or an SSH tunnel, keep metrics endpoints private, and use separate accounts with limited permissions.

I did not put student IDs, passwords, or request text into metric labels. Grouping by endpoint also keeps the number of labels manageable. I selected screenshots that do not show the student ID on my original app page. The app still uses Flask's development server, which I would need to replace and configure properly before using it in production.

To keep storage use down, Prometheus keeps two days of metrics and Docker rotates the container logs. Prometheus and Grafana are open source, but the Google VM, disk, network traffic, and public IP can still cost money. Once my screenshots and files were saved, I deleted the lab resources.

Conclusion

This project helped me see what monitoring adds to an app that is already running. I could generate requests and see the traffic, errors, and response times change on the dashboard. Prometheus handled collecting the metrics, and Grafana made them easier to compare. If I continued working on this setup, my next steps would be secure access and alerts for availability or high error rates.

Official references

  • Prometheus overview
  • Prometheus Docker installation
  • Prometheus configuration
  • PromQL functions
  • Prometheus Flask Exporter project documentation
  • Grafana provisioning
  • Google Cloud VPC firewall rules

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run on the Ubuntu VM: bash observability/deploy.sh
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
ROOT="$PWD"

# Prepare and validate before replacing any running containers.
sudo docker build -t student-app:monitoring .
sudo docker pull prom/prometheus:latest
sudo docker pull grafana/grafana:latest
sudo docker run --rm --entrypoint /bin/promtool \
  -v "$ROOT/observability/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro" \
  prom/prometheus:latest check config /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml

for name in student-app prometheus grafana; do
  if sudo docker container inspect "${name}-previous" >;/dev/null 2>;&;1; then
    echo "Backup container ${name}-previous already exists. Stop here and review before deploying again."
    exit 1
  fi
done

read -rsp 'Choose a NEW Grafana admin password (at least 12 characters): ' ADMIN_PASSWORD
printf '\n'
if [ "${#ADMIN_PASSWORD}" -lt 12 ]; then
  echo 'Password too short. Nothing has been replaced.'
  exit 1
fi
umask 077
ENV_FILE="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f -- "$ENV_FILE"' EXIT
printf 'GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=%s\n' "$ADMIN_PASSWORD" >; "$ENV_FILE"
unset ADMIN_PASSWORD

sudo docker network inspect it3200-monitoring >;/dev/null 2>;&;1 || sudo docker network create it3200-monitoring
sudo docker volume create prometheus-data >;/dev/null
sudo docker volume create grafana-data >;/dev/null

# Keep stopped backups. Do not delete the old containers or their volumes.
for name in student-app prometheus grafana; do
  if sudo docker container inspect "$name" >;/dev/null 2>;&;1; then
    sudo docker stop "$name"
    sudo docker rename "$name" "${name}-previous"
  fi
done

sudo docker run -d --name student-app --restart unless-stopped \
  --network it3200-monitoring -p 3000:3000 \
  --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=3 student-app:monitoring

sudo docker run -d --name prometheus --restart unless-stopped \
  --network it3200-monitoring -p 9090:9090 \
  --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=3 \

  --config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml \

  --network it3200-monitoring -p 3001:3000 \
  --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=3 \
  --env-file "$ENV_FILE" \
  -e GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_USER=admin -e GF_USERS_ALLOW_SIGN_UP=false \
  -v grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana \
  -v "$ROOT/observability/grafana/provisioning:/etc/grafana/provisioning:ro" \
  -v "$ROOT/observability/grafana/dashboards:/var/lib/grafana/dashboards:ro" \
  grafana/grafana:latest

echo 'Containers started. Verify readiness, targets, and the dashboard before claiming success.'
sudo docker ps
sudo docker image inspect student-app:monitoring prom/prometheus:latest grafana/grafana:latest \
  --format '{{.Id}} {{json .RepoDigests}}' >; "$ROOT/observability/deployed-images.txt"

event_model_payload.headline: Monitoring My Flask App with Prometheus and Grafana
event_model_payload.summary:
Introduction

For an earlier IT 3200 assignment, I built a small Flask app and ran it in Docker on a Linux virtual machine. The app displays a simple HTML page. For this assignment, I added monitoring so I could see how many requests it received, whether any requests failed, and how long the app took to respond.

I used Google Compute Engine to host the app, Prometheus to collect metrics, and Grafana to display them. I tested the setup by sending requests to the app and checking whether the graphs changed.

Everything runs on one Linux VM called vm-it3200-m7. It has three Docker containers: student-app, prometheus, and grafana. This was a small class project, so I kept the setup on one server.

Why Prometheus and Grafana?

I chose Prometheus because I had already used it in the Cloud Watching assignment. It checks a metrics endpoint at regular intervals and saves the numbers over time. Its query language, PromQL, lets me look at things like request counts and response times. Those were useful measurements for my Flask app.

I added Grafana so I could see several graphs together instead of running each query separately. Prometheus collects and stores the metrics, and Grafana reads that data to build the dashboard.

Google Cloud's monitoring service would have been another option, but Prometheus let me build on the work I had already done. Loki or the Elastic Stack would make more sense if I wanted to search through logs. For this project, I focused on request counts, errors, and response times.

There are limits to this setup. Checking every 15 seconds can miss short problems between checks, and the app's counters reset when its process restarts. I also did not add tracing or a central log system. Since everything is on one VM, a VM failure would take down both the app and its monitoring tools.

Architecture

The firewall rule allows my public IPv4 address using a /32 range and applies to the VM through the it3200-m7 network tag. I used port 3000 for Flask, 9090 for Prometheus, and 3001 for Grafana. Grafana uses port 3000 inside its container, so Docker maps the VM's port 3001 to the container's port 3000.

The containers communicate through a Docker network called it3200-monitoring. Prometheus connects to http://student-app:3000/metrics, and Grafana connects to http://prometheus:9090. Docker lets them find each other by container name, so they do not need to use the VM's public IP to communicate. Someone with administrator access to Docker can still access these containers.

Prometheus saves its data in a Docker volume named prometheus-data and keeps it for two days. Grafana saves its settings in grafana-data. Replacing a container does not erase these volumes, but deleting the VM's storage would. That is why I saved my screenshots and configuration on my computer.

Installation and configuration

First, I installed Docker on the Ubuntu VM:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y docker.io curl
sudo systemctl enable --now docker

My app already had a Dockerfile using Python 3.11. It installs the packages in requirements.txt, copies the app files, and runs python app.py on port 3000. I reused that Dockerfile.

I added this dependency to requirements.txt:

prometheus-flask-exporter==0.23.2

Then I added the exporter right after creating the Flask app:

from flask import Flask, render_template
from prometheus_flask_exporter import PrometheusMetrics

app = Flask(__name__)
metrics = PrometheusMetrics(app, group_by='endpoint')

This adds a /metrics page that Prometheus can read. The group_by setting groups request times by the Flask endpoint instead of every possible URL. The exporter also leaves its own metrics requests out of the default request measurements. Otherwise, checking the app could look like extra user traffic.

I configured Prometheus to check two targets every 15 seconds:

global:
  scrape_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: prometheus
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9090']
  - job_name: flask-app
    metrics_path: /metrics
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['student-app:3000']

The first target is Prometheus itself, which I used for Cloud Watching. The second is my Flask app. One thing I learned was that seeing Prometheus marked UP does not automatically mean it is collecting data from the app too.

I rebuilt the application and created the Docker network:

sudo docker build -t student-app:monitoring .
sudo docker network create it3200-monitoring

I used observability/deploy.sh to start the containers. The script builds the app and checks the Prometheus configuration with promtool check config. It also stops and renames the previous containers so they are kept as backups. The new containers use the shared Docker network and saved data volumes. Docker logs are limited to three 10 MB files per container to help prevent them from filling the disk.

These are the Prometheus settings for the configuration file, storage, and retention:

-v "$PWD/observability/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro"
-v prometheus-data:/prometheus
--config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
--storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus
--storage.tsdb.retention.time=2d

These lines are part of the Docker command, so they should not be run by themselves. The full script is included at the end of this post. If the containers or network already exist, check their names before running the commands again.

I used this file to tell Grafana where to find Prometheus:

apiVersion: 1
datasources:
  - name: Prometheus
    uid: prometheus
    type: prometheus
    access: proxy
    url: http://prometheus:9090
    isDefault: true
    editable: false
    jsonData:
      timeInterval: 15s

Grafana loads this file from /etc/grafana/provisioning/datasources. Another configuration file loads the dashboard JSON from /var/lib/grafana/dashboards. This saves the dashboard setup in files so I can recreate it without setting up every panel by hand.

I included the full script and monitoring files at the end of this post. Each code block shows where to save the file in the app project.

I used the latest Docker tags for Prometheus and Grafana. The script records the downloaded image IDs and digests in deployed-images.txt. Since latest can change, using those recorded digests would be a better way to repeat the setup with the exact same versions.

What the dashboard measures

The dashboard contains five panels:

Panel Purpose
Flask scrape availability Shows whether Prometheus can collect Flask metrics.
Requests per second Shows the rate of application HTTP requests.
HTTP errors per second Shows 4xx and 5xx response rates.
Mean response duration Shows mean server-side request processing time.
Requests by HTTP status Separates cumulative request counters by status code.

Request rate uses:

sum(rate(flask_http_request_total{job="flask-app"}[1m]))

The request counter keeps increasing as requests come in. rate uses the last minute of samples to estimate requests per second. It can account for a counter resetting, but it needs more than one sample before it can show a rate.

Mean response duration uses the histogram's sum and count:

sum(rate(flask_http_request_duration_seconds_sum{job="flask-app"}[1m]))
/
sum(rate(flask_http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="flask-app"}[1m]))

The duration metric measures how long the server takes to process requests. It does not include the full time a browser waits over the internet. The graph can have gaps when there are no requests. I created dashboards for this project but did not set up automatic alerts.

Showing it working

The Docker output shows all three containers running, and the readiness request returns Prometheus Server is Ready.

The up query returned 1 for both Prometheus and Flask, showing that both could be scraped. Grafana is not listed here because it reads data from Prometheus instead of being a scrape target in my setup.

To test it, I sent 120 requests to the home page with a half-second pause between requests. Then I sent ten requests to /missing-page. That page does not exist, so it returns a 404. This gave me a simple way to check whether errors appeared on the dashboard.

for i in $(seq 1 120); do
  curl -fsS http://localhost:3000/ > /dev/null
  sleep 0.5
done

for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000/missing-page
  sleep 1
done

In the screenshot, Flask scrape availability stays at 1 across the displayed samples. Around 22:17, the request rate peaks at about 1.9 requests per second and then drops to about 0.4 as the test finishes. The status graph shows about 120 successful responses and ten 404 responses. These numbers are estimates from reading the graph.

The error graph starts at zero and then rises to about 0.11 errors per second during the missing-page test. The errors were expected because I requested a page that did not exist. The displayed rate is averaged over a one-minute window, which is why it is lower than the one request per second sent by the test.

The average response time is roughly 230–260 microseconds, or 0.23–0.26 milliseconds. Grafana displays these small values in microseconds even though the original metric uses seconds. The requests came from inside the VM and the app is simple, so this does not tell me how fast the app would be for users over the internet or under a much larger load. Empty sections of the rate and duration graphs can also mean there were not enough recent requests or samples.

The graphs matched the activity I generated: the request count increased, the missing-page requests showed up as 404s, and Prometheus continued collecting metrics. Browser visits can add requests too, so I would not expect the counters to match a test script exactly every time.

The updated app also passed three local checks: successful requests were counted and timed, missing pages were counted as 404s, and metrics scrapes did not inflate the app request count. I still needed the VM checks and screenshots to confirm that the containers and dashboard worked together.

Roadblocks and lessons learned

My first roadblock was getting the VM running again. I had deleted the previous Azure resource group to avoid costs. When I tried creating another VM, Azure blocked it because of a subscription region policy. I switched to Google Compute Engine and reused the same Dockerized app.

Another thing I learned was the difference between monitoring Prometheus and monitoring my app. Cloud Watching only needed Prometheus to monitor itself. Adding the Flask exporter and a second target let me see what the app was doing. I also learned why the target uses student-app:3000: inside the Prometheus container, localhost points back to Prometheus, not Flask.

Security and cost considerations

I restricted the firewall rule to my public IPv4 address and the ports needed for the lab. Grafana requires an admin password, and new account sign-ups are disabled. I entered the password when running the script instead of saving it in the code. Someone with Docker administrator access could still inspect container settings, so this is not a complete solution for storing production secrets.

This setup uses HTTP, so restricting the source IP does not encrypt the connection. For a longer-term deployment, I would use HTTPS or an SSH tunnel, keep metrics endpoints private, and use separate accounts with limited permissions.

I did not put student IDs, passwords, or request text into metric labels. Grouping by endpoint also keeps the number of labels manageable. I selected screenshots that do not show the student ID on my original app page. The app still uses Flask's development server, which I would need to replace and configure properly before using it in production.

To keep storage use down, Prometheus keeps two days of metrics and Docker rotates the container logs. Prometheus and Grafana are open source, but the Google VM, disk, network traffic, and public IP can still cost money. Once my screenshots and files were saved, I deleted the lab resources.

Conclusion

This project helped me see what monitoring adds to an app that is already running. I could generate requests and see the traffic, errors, and response times change on the dashboard. Prometheus handled collecting the metrics, and Grafana made them easier to compare. If I continued working on this setup, my next steps would be secure access and alerts for availability or high error rates.

Official references

  • Prometheus overview
  • Prometheus Docker installation
  • Prometheus configuration
  • PromQL functions
  • Prometheus Flask Exporter project documentation
  • Grafana provisioning
  • Google Cloud VPC firewall rules

title: Sloth Fridge: A Fridge Photo Turns Into a Shopping List
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

I built Sloth Fridge. You take one photo of your fridge and it gives you a shopping list.

Here is the chore it removes. You open the fridge, the cold air is on your legs, you are staring at half a lemon and a tub of something, and you are trying to remember what you already bought. Then you write a list on your phone, you forget half of it in the shop, and you come home with three bags of the same thing.

Now you take one photo and close the door. While you are out, a small AI model that runs on your own laptop looks at the photo, works out what you have, compares it with what you had last time, and tells you what has run out. When you get home, the list is waiting for you.

It also reads your shopping receipt. Everything on the receipt gets ticked off and added to your pantry, so the list does not ask for milk right after you bought milk.

The people who get to be lazy here are anyone who shops. It is most useful for people who cook at home and shop for one or two people, because those are the people who end up buying the same six things every week.

Demo

There is no live link and no video, because the whole point is that it runs on your own machine and there is nothing to host.

The repo has four real fridge photos and a sample receipt. You can run the whole thing on your laptop with one command:

git clone https://github.com/sonu7089/sloth-fridge.git
cd sloth-fridge
pip install -e .
ollama pull qwen2.5vl:3b
ollama pull qwen2.5:3b
python scripts/demo.py

This is real output from my machine. It scanned four fridge photos in about 40 seconds each and printed the list:

scanning fridge-01-inside-double-sided-refrigerator.jpg ...
  19 item(s) in 56s
    - hot sauce x4 piece [condiment]
    - mustard x2 container [condiment]
    - mayo x2 pack [condiment]
    - yogurt x1 container [dairy]
    - milk x3 container [dairy]
    - soy sauce x2 container [condiment]
    - tomato ketchup x1 container [condiment]
    - eggs x6 pack [eggs]
    - bread x1 loaf [bread]
    - cheese x1 pack [dairy]
    ...

DAIRY
  [ ] butter x2 pack  (out of stock)
  [ ] milk x2 container  (running low, 1 container left)
  [ ] yogurt x2 container  (running low, 1 container left)

Morning digest
corn, cucumber, lemon, hot sauce
fridge smells like a tropical fruit salad

Then it reads the receipt and everything on it is ticked off:

bought milk
bought yogurt
bought eggs
bought cheese
bought bread
bought banana
bought lime
bought olive oil
bought tomato ketchup
bought black pepper
bought coffee

You can also drive it from the command line:

sloth-fridge scan fridge.jpg          # scan a photo
sloth-fridge list                      # show the list
sloth-fridge digest                    # two line morning summary
sloth-fridge receipt receipt.jpg       # read a receipt
sloth-fridge watch ~/Pictures/fridge   # scan new photos as they arrive

There is a web version too:

streamlit run sloth_fridge/ui.py

Code

https://github.com/sonu7089/sloth-fridge

How I Built It

These are the open source parts I used:

  • Ollama runs the models locally on my RTX 4060.
  • qwen2.5vl:3b looks at the photo. Apache 2.0, about 3.2 GB.
  • qwen2.5:3b turns notes into a shopping list. Apache 2.0, about 2 GB.
  • Pillow cuts the photo into tiles.
  • SQLite holds the pantry and the list.

Here is the thing that took me the longest, and it is the reason this project works at all.

qwen2.5vl:3b is a small model. When I asked it for JSON straight away, it broke. It made up one item and then repeated it twenty times:

{"items": [{"name": "jalapeno jelly", "qty": 1}, {"name": "jalapeno jelly", "qty": 1}, ...]}

It was not really looking at the photo either. The fix was three things.

One, let the model talk instead of making it fill in a form. I asked the same question in plain English, "look at this photo of a refrigerator shelf and tell me which food you can actually see", and the answer changed completely. It gave me "Mustard, Ketchup, Hot sauce, Pickles, Kikkoman soy sauce, Honey", and all of those really were in the photo. So now the vision model writes notes and the text model takes notes. Two jobs, two models.

Two, cut the photo into small tiles. A small carton at the back of a shelf is invisible in one wide photo. So I cut the photo into a 3 by 3 grid of overlapping tiles and look at each one. Then the votes decide. An item that shows up in three tiles is real. An item that shows up in one tile gets asked about again.

Three, do the boring work in normal Python. Brand names, pack sizes, units and vague answers like "yellow lid" are handled by code, not by the model. The model gives me "Kikkoman soy sauce", the code turns that into "soy sauce", and "free range eggs 12" becomes "eggs".

The rule I ended up with is simple. The model is good at seeing. It is bad at formats and bad at counting. So let it see, and let the code do the rest.

After all of that, a scan takes about 40 seconds on my laptop.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open is the reason this project is possible, not just nice to have.

It works with no internet. There is no API key and no bill. Pull the two models once and the tool works on a plane or on a cheap second hand laptop. A closed vision API charges you for every photo and needs a working connection every time.

Your fridge stays on your fridge. A photo of your fridge tells people your diet, your money, your health and your family. Uploading it to a company you do not control means sending it somewhere you do not control. My code makes exactly one network call and it goes to 127.0.0.1, which is my own Ollama process. You can check that yourself:

grep -rn "https\?://" sloth_fridge/
# config.py:50: OLLAMA_HOST = os.environ.get("OLLAMA_HOST", "http://127.0.0.1:11434")

It costs nothing to run. After the first download the cost of a scan is zero, so I can scan every single day. With a paid API, the thing I would use most is the thing that costs the most.

I could fix the model because the model was a file. The hallucination loop above was not a support ticket. I changed the prompt, I changed the sampling, I built a whole pipeline around it, and I can try a different checkpoint with one command:

SLOTH_VISION_MODEL=qwen2.5vl:7b sloth-fridge scan fridge.jpg

With a closed API I can only change the prompt. With an open model I can change how the model is used.

It is mine. The list of things I always keep stocked is a JSON file I own. Nobody can change what ends up on my shopping list, because there is no app running on someone else's server.

To be honest, a big closed model would read a fridge photo better than a 3B model does. What open wins for me here is privacy, cost, and the fact that I can fix it myself.

The Lazy Payoff

title: An Approval Queue for an AI-Supervised Agency: Routing Exceptions in Python
summary:
If an agency becomes a supervisor, the key piece of software is an approval queue: agents run routine work, and anything outside the rules waits for a person. This post sketches that in Python. It is an illustration, not a customer story, and I have no results to share.

The idea follows public advice from Google and BCG that agents handle repeatable work, while people set guardrails and review exceptions.

1. Rules the agent must follow 

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Rules:
    max_daily_budget_change_pct: float = 10.0
    needs_legal_review: tuple = ("guarantee", "cure", "risk-free", "best in")
    allowed_channels: tuple = ("search", "email")

2. Decide: auto-run or send to a person 

def route(action: dict, rules: Rules) -> str:
    text = action.get("copy", "").lower()
    if any(p in text for p in rules.needs_legal_review):
        return "legal_review"
    if action["channel"] not in rules.allowed_channels:
        return "account_manager"
    if abs(action.get("budget_change_pct", 0)) > rules.max_daily_budget_change_pct:
        return "account_manager"
    return "auto"

3. The queue and the log 

import json, time
queue = []

def submit(action, rules, log="decisions.jsonl"):
    lane = route(action, rules)
    if lane != "auto":
        queue.append({"action": action, "lane": lane})
    with open(log, "a") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps({"ts": time.time(), "lane": lane,
                            "action": action.get("name")}) + "\n")
    return lane

def approve(item, who, ok, log="decisions.jsonl"):
    with open(log, "a") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps({"ts": time.time(), "approved_by": who,
                            "ok": ok, "action": item["action"].get("name")}) + "\n")

What this shows

Routine actions run. Anything with a risky claim, an odd channel or a big budget jump goes to a named person, and every decision is logged. The supervisor's job is the rules in step 1 and the judgment in step 3.

Limits

String matching will miss things. A real setup needs proper review and your own legal advice. Treat this as a sketch.

Tej Pandya, founder of GrowEasy.ai.

title: Homebrew Was Using 25.6 GB of My Mac. Anaconda's Cache Alone Was 5 GB.
summary:
Last week I found AI coding tools hiding 32 GB on my MacBook. Claude, Codex, Cursor and Gemini were all sitting inside the grey "System Data" bar that macOS won't let you open.

So I kept going. The next biggest thing in there wasn't an app at all. It was Homebrew: 25.6 GB in /opt/homebrew.

I don't think of Homebrew as big. You type brew install, something appears, you move on. But every install leaves things behind, and a few of them are enormous.

Anaconda: 9.17 GB, and 5.21 GB of it is a cache

I installed Anaconda once for a data course. It's still here: 9.17 GB, plus an 882 MB copy of its installer that Homebrew keeps.

More than half of that, 5.21 GB, is anaconda3/pkgs: a copy of every package conda has ever downloaded, kept so the next install is faster. Your environments don't need it.

conda clean --all

That removes the cached packages and tarballs and leaves your environments alone. If you don't use conda anymore at all:

brew uninstall --cask anaconda

That's the whole 9.17 GB plus the installer copy.

Flutter: 4.1 GB

The Flutter SDK lives in /opt/homebrew/share/flutter. If you build Flutter apps, keep it. If you tried it once, brew uninstall --cask flutter gives back 4 GB.

Three Java versions: about 1 GB

I had openjdk, openjdk@17 and openjdk@11 installed side by side. Before removing an old one, check what still depends on it:

brew uses --installed openjdk@11

If that prints nothing, it's safe to brew uninstall openjdk@11.

Things you installed once and forgot

Hadoop (1.59 GB), MongoDB, Pandoc, Go. Each one was a reason at the time. This lists only the packages you installed, not their dependencies, which makes forgotten ones easy to spot:

brew leaves

The two commands everyone should run 

brew cleanup --prune=all   # old versions and every cached download
brew autoremove            # dependencies nothing needs anymore

Neither touches anything you still use.

Why macOS calls this "System Data"

/opt/homebrew isn't in your home folder, so macOS's Storage settings can't put it under Apps or Documents. It goes into System Data, alongside app caches and AI models. On my Mac, "Shared Library & Homebrew" alone was 32 GB of the 147 GB System Data bar.

The rule I follow now: caches are always safe, SDKs you don't use are the biggest wins, and anything with your data in it is a decision you make on purpose.

I build Tidy Mac, which is how I measured all of this. It breaks System Data into named parts like this one, and anything you clear goes to the Trash first. The commands above work without it.

Drafted with AI assistance. Every number was measured on my own Mac.

title: 用 Python 读取短信报价：整数金额、超时与 429 的处理
summary:
我在运营 RaySMS。本文由 AI 辅助编写，示例行为已按公开源码和离线测试核对。这里讨论一个不需要账户或 API Key 的只读命令行工具：用 Python 标准库读取服务、国家与报价，不购买号码，不触发或批量发送短信。

接入 OpenAI/ChatGPT/Codex、Google 或 Telegram 等服务前，先检查目录数据是一个独立步骤；出现报价并不保证目标平台接受号码或一定收到验证码。本文只关注如何让查询结果和失败状态足够明确。

1. 金额保留整数，展示时再转换

接口的 price_micros 以百万分之一美元表示金额。示例保留原整数，用 Decimal 生成六位小数字符串：

from decimal import Decimal

micros = 1000001
price_usd = format(Decimal(micros) / Decimal(1000000), ".6f")
# "1.000001"；这是测试数值，不是实时报价

不要先转成浮点数，也不要在排序前四舍五入到两位。很小的报价可能显示成零，随后失去比较价值。工具同时输出整数 price_micros 和字符串 price_usd，按整数排序。

输入校验也有细节：Python 的 bool 是 int 的子类，因此代码用 type(micros) is int，并拒绝负数、字符串和浮点报价。字段类型变化时明确报错，比悄悄转换更容易排查。

2. 一次报价查询并不只有一个请求

在仓库目录运行，需 Python 3.10 或更新版本，无第三方依赖：

python raysms_catalog.py --list services --lang zh-CN --limit 20
python raysms_catalog.py --service tg --format json --limit 10 --timeout 15

第二条先读服务和国家目录，再读报价，共三个 GET；无效国家编号会在报价请求前被拒绝。--limit 只限制输出行数，不减少接口返回的数据；设为零表示输出全部已返回的行，不会发起翻页请求。

--timeout 15 用于每次网络请求，不是整个程序十五秒内必然结束的承诺。工具保留默认 TLS 证书校验，并限制单个响应为 2 MiB，还会检查 JSON 结构，防止把错误页面当成空库存。

3. 遇到 429，先停下来

示例收到 HTTP 429 会显示 Retry-After（如果服务端提供），退出且不自动重试。网络或 TLS 失败也返回简短错误，不打印原始响应体或内部诊断内容。

如果将来接入定时任务，应遵守服务端等待提示，设置有限重试次数并减少查询频率；这属于调用方需要增加的策略，当前 CLI 没有实现自动退避。查询失败也不能据此推断“某国家没有库存”。正常空结果与请求失败必须分别处理。

4. 先运行八项离线测试 

python -m unittest -v

测试替换网络调用，覆盖公开 GET 不带凭据、拒绝未知路径、微美元精度、错误金额类型、429 不重试、无效 JSON 或结构、诊断信息隐藏，以及无效国家提前停止。本轮八项均通过，但这些测试不代表实时库存或平台接受率测试。

可以从 GitHub 完整源码与测试 复现，也可以用 Postman 公开只读集合 查看请求。更完整的字段说明见 RaySMS Python 接入指南。公开查询阶段无需放入任何密钥，后续涉及付费操作时，应另行设计授权与金额核验。

title: Constant State Detection in Time Series with Python.
summary:
Constant State Detection in Time Series with Python.

See this code on Github

In this article we will detect constant state section in time series with Python.

You can take a look at the preprint with the introduction to the algorithm here.

We will use the package that requires Python 3.10+

Installation:

Recommended:

1. Create a virtual environment.

For Linux: execute the console command

python3 -m venv your_path_to_new_virtual_environment

for other operation systems there could be different command(s)

2. Activate it.

For Linux: execute the console command

source your_path_to_new_virtual_environment/bin/activate

for other operation systems there could be different command(s)

3. Install the package.

execute the console command

pip install csd-algo

Quick check if it is working

now execute the console command

python -m csd_algo.usage_example

If all have been done correctly, you should see the console output and a couple of plots like this:

Example figure:

Now create the github_example.py file and paste the following code into it: 


import requests
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from csd_algo.client_axiliary import report_results, __version__
from csd_algo.models import (MAX_CSD_POINTS_FREE, CSD_Data,  
                    to_jsonable_dict)
from csd_algo.generate_timeseries_numpy import generate_timseries

plt.close('all')

url_csd_algo = 'https://dazzling-faithful-banteng.anvil.app/constant-state-detection'

ts: list[float] = generate_timseries(
    0.5, 
    MAX_CSD_POINTS_FREE,
    ).tolist()

# process the timeseries with the default settings:

csd_data = CSD_Data(csd_algo_input=ts, 
                    csd_algo_min_window_width=16, 
                    csd_algo_max_window_height=0.08)

# send the data to the server and receive the reply
response = requests.post(url_csd_algo, 
                         json=to_jsonable_dict(csd_data))

# validate received data
out_data = CSD_Data.model_validate(response.json())

# print and plot the processing results
report_results(out_data, 
               f'CSD plot, Algorithm type: postprocessing')

print(f'Client version is {__version__}')

Save the file and execute the console command

python github_example.py

Now you should see some console output and just one plot like the picture above.

After completing and verifying these steps, you can adjust the input data and algorithm parameters to test the algorithm implementation according to your requirements.

    """
    class to hold the Constant State Detection algorithm data
    #
    values:
    #

    csd_algo_min_window_width: int
    csd_algo_max_window_height: float
    Algo_Type: AlgorithmType = AlgorithmType.POSTPROCESSING_V1
    Window_Height_Type: WindowHeightType = WindowHeightType.Relative
    start: list[int] = []
    finish: list[int] = []
    start_section_series: list[int] = []
    finish_section_series: list[int] = []

The main parameters here are:

  • csd_algo_input: list[float] - this is the timeseries input data for the algorithm
  • csd_algo_min_window_width: int - this is the minimal window width input for the algorithm
  • csd_algo_max_window_height: float - this is the maximal window height input for the algorithm

It is better to leave the parameters Algo_Type and Window_Height_Type values to have their default values for the beginning. Algo_Type.POSTPROCESSING_V1 value means advanced algorithm which chooses the 'best' constant state section with the minimal height from sections that have the maximal length from one continuous constant state section series.

It might also be helpful to take a look at the code to create the numpy array used for testing: 


def generate_timseries(b: float, points_cnt: int=256, 
                       periods: int=1, 
                       phi: float = 0) -> np.array:
        """
        function to generate the test timeseries for the 
        constant state detection algorithm demo. returns the 
        float numpy arrray with the sin(x) + b * sin(2 * x + phi)
        sum of the first and the second harmonic inside.

        input parameters:
        * b - float, the value of the second harmonic
        * points_cnt - int, the count of the points in the output array
        * periods - int, the period count of the first harmonic
        * phi - float, the phase of the second harmonic in the radians, multiplied by the PI value
        """

        points = int(periods * points_cnt)
        phase = phi * np.pi
        x = np.arange(points)
        y = np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * periods * x / points)
        sin2 = b * np.sin(4.0 * np.pi * periods * x / points + phase)
        y += sin2
        return y

Using these definitions, one can easily test the algorithm with one's own input data; for example load them from a file, just don't forget about the MAX_CSD_POINTS_FREE input point count restriction.

Important note: Unfortunately, I can't guarantee at the moment that the webservice will work with the good uptime and response time, as this is just a free test version of the webservice. There might be times when the webservice will be inaccessible for hours, maybe even for days.

title: 48-Hour Field Notes: My Oldest Answer Won the Cache Because I Trusted Arrival Order
summary:
I spent last weekend convinced my summarizer was lying to me, and for once the model was innocent.

The worker sent eight requests for the same document, kept whichever response came back last, and wrote it to the cache, because that is what "last write wins" means when you never question what "last" refers to. By Saturday afternoon the cache held a summary of version 2 of a document that was already on version 9, and every downstream reader was quietly reading stale prose. So let me ask the obvious question I failed to ask on Friday: when you say the result arrived last, do you mean the request finished last, or that the work started last?

What I Actually Built, and What It Cost Me

I pointed a small worker at MonkeyCode's free model access, which the operator supplies as an available option, and ran the worker itself on the free server option so I would not have to babysit a laptop all weekend. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. I did not benchmark either side, I did not record model-side latency numbers, and everything below is about my own worker's bookkeeping rather than about anyone's infrastructure.

The pipeline was boring on purpose: a queue of document revisions, one call per revision, one cache write per response, and a rewrite rule that said newer wins. I had already learned to hash inputs so I could tell whether a run had actually happened, and I had a replay cassette for repeatability, so I felt reasonably grown-up about the whole thing. Then I opened the cache on Saturday morning and read a summary that mentioned a paragraph I had deleted nine hours earlier.

The Assumption That Broke: Arrival Order Is Not Logical Order

Concurrency does not preserve your send order, and neither does any retry layer you bolt on top of it, which means "last response wins" is a rule about wall-clock arrival and not about freshness. The eighth revision can finish first because it was short, and the second revision can finish last because it hit a slow path and got retried twice, and your cache will faithfully record the older answer. Is that a model problem, a network problem, or a bookkeeping problem? It was the third one, and it was mine.

Here is the shape of the bug, stripped of my domain code:

  • Revision 8 finishes at T+2s and writes summary = v8.
  • Revision 2, still in flight, finishes at T+9s and writes summary = v2.
  • Every reader after T+9s sees the older revision, and nothing errors, logs, or alerts.

Artifact 1: A Ticket Guard Instead of a Timestamp

Wall-clock timestamps did not save me, because two hosts disagreed by enough to invert the comparison, and because I was comparing the wrong moment anyway. What worked was stamping each job with a monotonically increasing ticket taken from the enqueue side, then refusing any commit whose ticket is not newer than the last committed one for that key.

# guard.py
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Commit:
    ticket: int
    key: str
    value: str

class LastWriterGuard:
    """Rejects stale commits per key. Tickets must come from the enqueue side."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._seen: dict[str, int] = {}
        self.rejected = 0
        self.accepted = 0

    def commit(self, c: Commit) -> bool:
        previous = self._seen.get(c.key)
        if previous is not None and c.ticket <= previous:
            self.rejected += 1
            return False
        self._seen[c.key] = c.ticket
        self.accepted += 1
        # real code writes to Redis/SQLite/Postgres here
        return True

Fifteen lines, no dependencies, and the counter is the part I actually care about, because a rejection count above zero on a quiet afternoon tells me something is reordering. The same idea survives a restart if you put the comparison in the write itself:

UPDATE summaries
   SET value = :value, ticket = :ticket, updated_at = now()
 WHERE doc_key = :key
   AND ticket < :ticket;
-- zero rows affected means you lost the race on purpose, which is fine

Artifact 2: Reproduce the Reorder Without Touching a Network

The reason I trusted my old code for as long as I did is that the bug is invisible when calls are fast and uniform, so I wrote a test that fabricates the arrival order instead of waiting for it. The delays are synthetic, chosen to put the lowest ticket last, and the point is the assertion rather than the numbers.

# test_reorder.py
import asyncio
from guard import Commit, LastWriterGuard

TICKETS = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
# ticket 1 finishes almost instantly, ticket 2 finishes last
DELAYS = [0.05, 0.90, 0.30, 0.20, 0.40, 0.10, 0.60, 0.15]

async def fake_call(ticket: int, delay: float, guard: LastWriterGuard, log: list):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)  # stand-in for an HTTP round trip
    ok = guard.commit(Commit(ticket, "doc:42", f"v{ticket}"))
    log.append((ticket, ok))

async def run() -> tuple[list, LastWriterGuard]:
    guard, log = LastWriterGuard(), []
    await asyncio.gather(*(fake_call(t, d, guard, log) for t, d in zip(TICKETS, DELAYS)))
    return log, guard

def test_guard_blocks_stale_last_arrival():
    log, guard = asyncio.run(run())
    assert log[-1] == (2, False), "stale revision 2 arrived last and was rejected"
    assert guard.accepted == 4
    assert guard.rejected == 4

python -m pytest -q test_reorder.py
# 1 passed

Delete the guard and the last write becomes v2, which is exactly what my cache contained on Saturday morning. I ran this across a few hundred shuffled delay vectors with a random seed, and the guard never let a lower ticket overwrite a higher one, which is a weak property but a property I can state out loud.

The Second Failure: I Stamped the Ticket in the Wrong Place

My first version attached the ticket at send time, which meant a retry got a brand new ticket and politely re-committed older content as if it were fresh. The fix was to move the stamp to the enqueue step and carry it through every retry unchanged, so a retried ticket 2 stays ticket 2 forever. Did the guard hide work rather than save it? Partly, yes: rejected commits are wasted calls, and the rejection counter is now my cheapest signal that I am paying for answers I throw away.

Where This Guard Is the Wrong Tool

Situation Use this Why
One producer, one key, retries Enqueue-side ticket guard Cheap, monotonic, survives restarts
Several producers writing one key Database sequence or a single writer service Local tickets do not give a total order
Duplicate delivery, same payload Idempotency key on the request Guard rejects nothing useful
Strict ordering required Serialize per key in a queue No concurrency, no reordering

Limitations and Who Should Skip This

If your pipeline is already sequential per document, this guard buys you a branch and a dictionary lookup, and nothing else. If several machines enqueue jobs for the same key without a shared sequence, a per-process counter will happily accept the wrong order, so use a database sequence instead. And if downstream readers can observe a value mid-flight, the guard does not help, because the stale value was visible before the newer one ever landed.

I would repeat two things: stamping freshness at the enqueue step, and writing the reorder test before writing the fix. What I would not repeat is the assumption that finishing last means thinking last, because on a weekend with free model access and a free server option, the only thing I actually saved was the budget for one more bad assumption. If you keep your own field notes, the rejection counter is a good first line to add this week.

title: Nothing Failed. The Suite Just Got Slower: A Wall-Clock Budget Gate for Agent Patches
summary:
A patch touches zero test files. No assertion changes, no new skips, no fixture edits. The suite goes green on the first run.

Then someone opens the job duration graph and the branch takes nearly three times as long as the commit it branched from.

Numbers in this post are illustrative unless labelled otherwise. The mechanism is the point, not the magnitudes.

Conclusion first: wall-clock duration, retry consumption, and runner configuration are test surfaces in exactly the same sense that assertions and fixtures are. Diff them with two ledgers, gate on ratios rather than absolutes, and attach an expiry date to every exception. The rest of this article is machinery for that sentence.

Why the usual patch audits stay silent

Most patch review looks at the test tree: assertions added or removed, fixture write sets, verdict flips between base and head, co-movement between fixture and assertion. All of that is content.

Duration inflation is behaviour. It usually lands outside the test tree entirely — a raised timeout value, a retries plugin configured to 3, a sleep(0.5) inserted into shared setup code, a marker that quietly turns a slow integration test into a CI skip.

title: Mercury 3 Does 1,068 Tokens/Second With a Diffusion LLM — Here's the Architecture Trick (and How to Try It)
summary:
Today Inception Labs dropped Mercury 3: a diffusion-based LLM with a 1M-token context window doing 1,068 tokens/sec on NVIDIA GPUs, claiming to beat GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on benchmarks — at $0.20/$0.70 per million tokens, half price during launch. It's live on OpenRouter, Baseten, Vercel, and behind an OpenAI-compatible API, so you can try it by changing a base URL.

If you're a builder, here's the part that matters: this is not "a faster autoregressive model." It's a different generation paradigm, and it changes what your inference code can assume.

The 30-second architecture primer

Autoregressive decoding: for i in range(n): token[i] = model(tokens[:i]). Serial. Unfixable — once token 5 is emitted, it's baked in.

Diffusion decoding: start with a fully masked/noisy sequence of length n, then iteratively denoise all positions in parallel over K refinement steps. Position 5 can be revised in step 12 based on what position 500 looks like. The model gets K parallel passes over the whole sequence instead of n serial commits.

That parallelism is where 1,068 tok/s comes from. On a GPU, parallel refinement across the sequence exploits the hardware's actual strength (wide vector math) instead of its weakness (serial dependency chains).

Why this should change your evals

Three workload classes where diffusion's architecture is structurally advantaged:

  1. Infilling and editing. Code completion mid-file, document revision, structured-output repair. Autoregressive models fake this with fill-in-the-middle hacks; diffusion models do it natively because every position is refinable.
  2. Constrained generation. JSON schemas, formats with global consistency requirements, anything where a late constraint should rewrite an early choice. Serial models can't go back; diffusion can.
  3. Self-correction loops. Exposure bias — the "one wrong token poisons everything downstream" problem — is an autoregressive artifact. Parallel refinement doesn't have it, at least not in the same form.

The flip side, from the research literature (Diffusion-LM, SEDD, LLaDA): open-ended long-form coherence and precise instruction-following have historically lagged autoregressive models. Mercury 3 claims to close the gap. Claims. Test it yourself.

Trying it: the 5-minute eval 

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.inception.ai/v1",  # OpenAI-compatible endpoint
    api_key="YOUR_INCEPTION_KEY",
)

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="mercury-3",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Refactor this function..."}],
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)

What to actually measure — don't just vibe-check:

  • Time to first usable token vs. full completion time. Diffusion models refine the whole sequence; "first token" semantics differ. Measure what your UX actually needs.
  • Throughput at YOUR context length, not the headline 1,068 tok/s (measured at favorable conditions). Plot tok/s against 4K / 32K / 128K / 1M context. The 1M-context + max-speed pairing is almost certainly not simultaneous.
  • Edit/infill accuracy on your real tasks: give it broken JSON, half-written functions, documents with a paragraph to rewrite. This is where diffusion should win — verify it does.
  • Instruction-following precision on multi-constraint prompts. This is where diffusion historically loses — verify it doesn't.

The honest caveats (day-one edition)

  • Vendor benchmarks, vendor hardware, vendor conditions. Independent evals will land in days; don't migrate production on launch-day numbers.
  • The entire inference ecosystem (KV-cache tricks, speculative decoding, every serving framework's optimizations) was built for autoregressive decoding. Diffusion uses different kernel patterns — expect immature tooling and surprising failure modes.
  • Prompt engineering behaves differently. Techniques tuned for left-to-right generation (chain-of-thought scaffolding, "let's think step by step") may not transfer. Budget time to re-learn what works.

Why I'm paying attention anyway

October has been the month the LLM monoculture cracked: open weights counter-attacking (816B-param models last week), inference prices collapsing (DeepSeek's $0.50 agent yesterday), and now a non-autoregressive architecture shipping at frontier-adjacent quality. Even if Mercury 3's numbers turn out optimistic, the direction is set — and the builders who understand diffusion decoding now will have a head start when (not if) every lab ships one.

Try it this week. Report back what breaks. That's how new architectures earn trust.

Source: Inception announcement via PANews, Oct 20, 2026. Benchmark figures are vendor-reported. Written by Shivam Kumar (VisionQuantech).

The artifact: a checker that refuses orphaned numbers

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# tools/doc_facts.py
"""Fail a docs build when a drafted number has no line of evidence."""

from __future__ import annotations

import datetime as dt
import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

FACTS = re.compile(r"", re.S)
NUM = re.compile(r"(?")


def parse_block(block: str) -> list[dict]:
    facts, cur = [], None
    for raw in block.splitlines():
        line = raw.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith("#"):
            continue
        if line.startswith("- "):
            cur = {}
            facts.append(cur)
            line = line[2:]
        if cur is None:
            continue
        key, _, value = line.partition(":")
        cur[key.strip()] = value.strip().strip('"').strip("'")
    return facts


def numbers(text: str) -> set[str]:
    return set(NUM.findall(text))


def window(repo: Path, rel: str, lineno: int, pad: int = 2) -> str:
    lines = (repo / rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
    lo = max(0, lineno - 1 - pad)
    hi = min(len(lines), lineno + pad)
    return "\n".join(lines[lo:hi])


def check(fact: dict, repo: Path, today: dt.date) -> list[str]:
    kind, text = fact.get("kind", ""), fact.get("text", "")
    fid = fact.get("id", "?")
    if kind == "code":
        rel, _, line = fact.get("source", "").partition(":")
        if not rel or not line.isdigit():
            return [f"{fid}: code fact needs source=path:line"]
        try:
            snippet = window(repo, rel, int(line))
        except OSError as exc:
            return [f"{fid}: cannot read {rel}: {exc}"]
        return [
            f"{fid}: {n!r} not in {rel}:{line} (+/-2 lines)"
            for n in numbers(text)
            if n not in snippet
        ]
    if kind == "external":
        errs = []
        if not fact.get("url", "").startswith("http"):
            errs.append(f"{fid}: external fact needs a url")
        try:
            age = (today - dt.date.fromisoformat(fact.get("retrieved", ""))).days
        except ValueError:
            return [f"{fid}: retrieved must be YYYY-MM-DD"]
        if age > 180:
            errs.append(f"{fid}: retrieved {age} days ago, refresh it")
        return errs
    if kind == "human":
        return [] if fact.get("owner") else [f"{fid}: human fact needs an owner"]
    return [f"{fid}: kind must be code, external, or human"]


def main(paths: list[str]) -> int:
    repo, fails = Path.cwd(), 0
    head = subprocess.run(
        ["git", "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD"],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True,
    ).stdout.strip()
    today = dt.date.today()
    for p in paths:
        doc = Path(p).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        block = FACTS.search(doc)
        if not block:
            stray = numbers(doc)
            if stray:
                print(f"{p}: numbers {sorted(stray)} without a facts block")
                fails += 1
            continue
        facts = parse_block(block.group(1))
        covered = set().union(*(numbers(f.get("text", "")) for f in facts))
        for fact in facts:
            for err in check(fact, repo, today):
                print(f"{p}: {err}")
                fails += 1
        for stray in sorted(numbers(FACTS.sub("", doc)) - covered):
            print(f"{p}: prose number {stray!r} has no fact entry")
            fails += 1
        print(f"{p}: {len(facts)} facts checked at {head}")
    return 1 if fails else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1:]))
